item.title: Amazon Quick adds unified conversational AI over structured and unstructured data
item.description:
Amazon Quick adds unified conversational AI over structured and unstructured data

Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Quick lets you connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3‑backed knowledge bases, then query both through a single conversational AI agent.

🧩 How it works

  • Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base.
  • Structured data (metrics, sales figures, operational KPIs) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL.
  • A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries, and can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors.
  • A custom chat agent links to the Space, uses it as its knowledge source, determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations.
  • AI guardrails such as content‑safety screening are applied to chat interactions.
  • Adding a new data source to the Space makes it instantly usable by the linked agent, while responses respect the permissions of the requesting user.

⚙️ Key Details

  • An Amazon Quick account with an Enterprise subscription is required to create datasets.
  • In the admin console, an administrator chooses Permissions → AWS resources → Amazon S3 → Select S3 buckets; selected buckets have read‑only permissions by default.
  • Permissions are needed to create integrations, knowledge bases, datasets, spaces, and chat agents.
  • Setup steps:
    1. Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket.
    2. In the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel.
    3. Choose the Amazon S3 connector and click Add.
    4. Provide the S3 bucket URL (the bucket must be in the same Region as Amazon Quick).
    5. Decide whether to use ACLs before creating the knowledge base (cannot be changed later).
    6. A success banner confirms the integration and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background.
    7. Load a structured file (e.g., Product_Sales.csv) as a dataset.
    8. Enrich the dataset with semantic descriptions, custom instructions, and correct data types so the AI can translate natural‑language questions into SQL.
  • The layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context is the Space.

🗂 Component Summary

Component Purpose
Knowledge Base Indexes unstructured content stored in Amazon S3 for AI‑powered search
Enriched Dataset Holds structured data with semantic descriptions; enables SQL translation
Space Workspace that references both the knowledge base and datasets; may include dashboards, file uploads, action connectors
Custom Chat Agent Links to a Space, decides which source(s) to query, returns combined response with citations
Permissions Controls access to S3 buckets, datasets, and ensures responses respect user permissions

🚀 Availability

  • Requires an Enterprise subscription for dataset creation.
  • The S3 bucket must reside in the same AWS Region as Amazon Quick.
  • All components (knowledge bases, datasets, spaces, chat agents) are created through the Amazon Quick console.

item.title: NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness
item.description:
NVIDIA KGMON Team Secures Second Place at KDD Cup 2026 with Agent Harness

The NVIDIA KGMON team placed second in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents competition with a system that streamlines the agent harness to be smaller, clearer, and easier to verify.

🔍 Overview

  • The competition required agents to answer natural‑language questions over heterogeneous data sources such as databases, CSV/JSON files, prose documents, PDFs, and briefing videos.
  • Every task demanded more than simple retrieval: agents had to inspect data, choose appropriate tools, reason across sources, produce a final answer file, and navigate traps common in analytical workflows.
  • Teams were limited to a small, fixed LLM, making the harness the primary optimization surface.
  • KGMON’s approach focused on preprocessing, constrained tools, persistent state, and systematic evaluation to make the task easier for the available model.

🛠️ Architecture & Workflow

  • Unified data access – CSV and JSON files were converted into tables inside a single SQLite database, giving the agent one SQL interface for all structured data.
  • Single tool set – The environment exposed only a few helpers: schema inspection, SQL queries, document lookup, prose extraction, and answer writing.
  • Schema‑scouting step – Before the main reasoning loop the system inspected tables, columns, join keys, duplicate names, units, null patterns, and row‑grain issues, then supplied this context to the agent.
  • Middleware repair – Malformed tool calls were automatically fixed so a single bad call would not abort the attempt.
  • Stateful Python environment – Variables persisted between tool calls, allowing reuse of intermediate results.
  • Predefined functions – schema(), sql(query), and write_answer(df) reduced boilerplate, syntax errors, and file‑handling mistakes.
  • Execution tracing – Repeated attempts and trajectory inspection helped identify failures and refine the harness.
Function / Helper Role
schema() Provide the agent with table and column metadata discovered during scouting
sql(query) Execute a SQL statement against the unified SQLite database
write_answer(df) Write the final answer file in the required format
Document lookup Retrieve relevant prose or PDF content
Prose extraction Pull specific text snippets from unstructured documents

Figure 1 (see below) illustrates the overall workflow from data ingestion to final answer generation.

⚙️ Reliability Techniques

  • Preprocessing data into a uniform SQL schema reduced routing failures and saved turns for reasoning.
  • Constrained tool set limited the ways the agent could interact with the environment, lowering the chance of mistakes.
  • Persistent state and middleware repair prevented a single error from ending an attempt.
  • Short, valid attempts conserved the limited turn budget for additional runs, evaluation, and ensembling.
  • Execution traces and trajectory inspection were used to pinpoint failures such as bad tool calls or answer‑format issues.

🚩 Common Failure Modes

  • Bad tool call (e.g., syntax error)
  • Incorrect join key leading to wrong results
  • Missed document rule or threshold in unstructured sources
  • Answer‑format mismatch causing the final output to be rejected

💡 Why It Matters

  • The techniques are especially useful when building reliable systems around smaller open models.
  • Reliability often stems more from a well‑designed harness than from expanding the openness of the model itself.
  • A streamlined harness leaves more capacity for the fixed LLM to focus on analysis rather than plumbing.
